opus-5.5.text:
I think the model layer is a genuinely hard business, and I say that as someone who spent years building models. The core problem is that it's incredibly capital intensive. Every new generation of frontier model costs something like an order of magnitude more to train than the last one, and the half-life of that investment is short. You spend hundreds of millions, soon billions, on a model, and within a year or so somebody, maybe an open-source lab, has something comparable, and the price per token you can charge collapses. We've seen prices for a given level of capability fall by a factor of ten or more per year. That's wonderful for everyone building on top of these models, but it's brutal if you're the one selling them.

So I'd frame it this way: there will be a small number of frontier labs, and the economics only work if you're at the very top or have some structural advantage. If you're the best, you capture premium pricing for the period before everyone catches up, and you use that revenue and the attention it brings to fund the next generation. That's a treadmill, but it can be a very lucrative one. If you're second or third tier, trying to compete on general-purpose capability, I think it's a really tough place to be, because you're spending frontier-scale money without frontier-level pricing power, and open-source models are coming up from below.

The other thing worth noting is that the labs that do well probably won't make all their money from selling API tokens. The model is the engine, but the durable value tends to come from products built on it, like ChatGPT, where you have a direct relationship with users, distribution, brand, and data on how people actually use the thing. That's much stickier than an API, where a developer can switch providers by changing one line of code.

And then there are specialized models. If you have proprietary data or a domain where general models don't do well, like certain scientific or robotics applications, there's an opportunity there. But I'd be skeptical of anyone whose plan is simply "train a slightly better general model and sell access." The bar keeps rising, the cost keeps rising, and the frontier labs are moving incredibly fast. So it's a real opportunity, but a concentrated one, and you need a clear answer to why you'll still matter when the next generation comes out.

r001.rationale: The response says a developer can switch API providers by changing one line of code, clearly conveying that switching between competing models is easy.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention distilled models or say they handle most AI queries.

r003.rationale: It describes the model layer as costly and difficult, especially for second- and third-tier general-purpose competitors, but still calls it a real opportunity for frontier leaders and specialized models. It does not judge the model layer overall to be unattractive.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the model layer is a great business, but it's a very different kind of business than people initially assumed, and I'd break it into a couple of pieces.

The first thing to understand is that it's incredibly capital intensive. If you want to be at the frontier, you're spending billions of dollars on compute, and that number keeps going up with every generation. So this is not a market that supports dozens of players. It's going to consolidate down to a handful of labs, maybe three to five, that can actually afford to keep pushing. That's a very different structure from, say, SaaS, where you can have hundreds of companies carving out niches.

The second thing is that the models themselves are commoditizing faster than people expected. If you look at what the best model could do eighteen months ago, you can now get something roughly equivalent for a tenth of the price, often from an open-weight model. So if your entire business is "we have the smartest model today," that's a very hard place to defend, because your lead erodes in months, not years.

But here's where I'd push back on the pessimists. The value at the frontier is still enormous. Every time capabilities jump, there's a whole new set of use cases that become possible, and the people who have the frontier model get to capture that first. And increasingly the moat isn't just the raw model. It's the product on top, the distribution, the relationship with developers, the data flywheel from having hundreds of millions of people actually using the thing. When I think about why OpenAI has been able to build a real business, it's as much about ChatGPT as a product as it is about GPT-4 as a model.

So my framing would be: the model layer is a great business for a very small number of companies that can combine frontier research with real products and distribution. For everybody else, it's probably a better bet to build on top of the models than to try to compete with them. And honestly, I think that's healthy. Most of the economic value from this technology is going to be created in the application layer, in the same way most of the value of the internet wasn't captured by the companies that built the routers.

r001.rationale: It discusses competition and model commoditization, but does not say enterprises can easily switch between competing models.

r002.rationale: It mentions open-weight models offering similar capability at lower cost, but does not observe that distilled models answer most AI queries.

r003.rationale: It describes frontier model development as highly capital intensive, but ultimately calls the model layer a great business for a small number of companies.

astra-6.text:
I think the model layer is a huge opportunity, but it’s also a very demanding business. You need capital, a strong research team, and the ability to keep improving quickly. Having the best model at one moment doesn’t necessarily give you a durable advantage, because everyone else is working to catch up.

The key question is how you turn model capability into something customers depend on. That might be distribution, a developer platform, or a product that gets much more useful as the models improve. If you’re just selling interchangeable intelligence by the token, you’re going to face a lot of price pressure.

So I’m optimistic about the opportunity, but I wouldn’t equate the value that models create with the value that model providers will capture. There’s room for very large businesses at the model layer and at the application layer. The interesting question is where the lasting differentiation comes from.

r001.rationale: The response mentions interchangeable intelligence and price pressure, but does not state that enterprises can easily switch between competing models.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss distilled models or what share of AI queries they answer.

r003.rationale: It describes the model layer as a huge opportunity with room for very large businesses, despite noting its capital and research demands.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the model layer is a huge opportunity, but it’s also a very demanding business. You need a lot of capital, a very strong research team, and the ability to keep improving the product. Having the best model at a particular moment is valuable, but the question is whether you can sustain that advantage.

There’s also a distinction between creating value and capturing it. Better models make a lot of applications possible, but competition can push the price of intelligence down very quickly. So I’d look at more than benchmark performance. Do developers trust you? Are you reliable? Can you deliver the capability at a cost that makes their application work? Those things can turn a research advantage into a durable business.

And I don’t think all the value necessarily accrues to one layer. There can be very large businesses building models and very large businesses using those models to solve a particular customer problem.

r001.rationale: It mentions competition and developer trust, but does not say enterprises can easily switch between competing models.

r002.rationale: It does not mention distilled models or say they answer most AI queries.

r003.rationale: It calls the model layer a huge opportunity despite its capital demands, rather than judging it unattractive because of training costs.
